blocks.overview: This case concerns the Minister's application to cease the refugee protection of a Cuban citizen who was previously recognized as a Convention refugee by the Refugee Protection Division (RPD). The Minister alleges the respondent voluntarily reavailed himself of Cuba's protection by obtaining a Cuban passport and returning to Cuba multiple times. The tribunal allowed the cessation application, rejecting the respondent's refugee claim under section 108 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act.

blocks.issue: Was it procedurally fair to proceed with the hearing in the respondent's absence?
blocks.court_conclusion: Proceeding in the respondent's absence did not breach procedural fairness due to his failure to update contact information.

positions.text: The respondent was aware of the cessation application and his duty to notify changes but was not diligent; efforts were made to locate him.
Rule 12 requires protected persons to notify changes in contact information without delay.

blocks.issue: Did the respondent voluntarily reavail himself of Cuba's protection, justifying cessation of refugee status under section 108(1)(a)?
blocks.court_conclusion: The respondent's early acquisition of a Cuban passport and multiple returns to Cuba show reavailment, justifying cessation under section 108(1)(a).

positions.text: Returned to Cuba for family reasons in 2011, 2013, and 2015; provided supporting documents; explanations accepted as credible.
Minister alleges passport obtained in 2009 and multiple returns to Cuba show voluntary reavailment.
Respondent voluntarily obtained passport before family illness and returned multiple times without Canadian permission, indicating reavailment.
UNHCR Handbook and Canadian jurisprudence presume obtaining a passport and returning to the country indicates reavailment and cessation of refugee status.
Respondent's reasons for returning do not rebut presumption of reavailment; no evidence of seeking Canadian permission or travel document.

propositions.text: The respondent is a Cuban citizen who came to Canada in October 2005 and claimed refugee protection.
On March 16, 2006, the respondent was determined to be a Convention refugee by the RPD.
The respondent became a permanent resident of Canada on January 30, 2007.

paragraphs.summary: The respondent is a Cuban citizen who claimed refugee protection in 2005, was recognized as a Convention refugee in 2006, and became a permanent resident in 2007.

propositions.text: This decision concerns the Minister's application to cease the respondent's refugee protection under section 108(2) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act.

paragraphs.summary: The court states this decision concerns the Minister's application to cease the respondent's refugee protection under section 108(2) of the Act.

propositions.text: On May 7, 2015, the RPD received the Minister's cessation application regarding the respondent's refugee status.
The Minister alleges the respondent was issued a Cuban passport in 2009 and returned to Cuba in 2011, 2013, and 2015.
The Minister alleges these actions show the respondent voluntarily reavailed himself of Cuba's protection, ceasing refugee status under section 108(1)(a).

paragraphs.summary: The Minister alleges the respondent obtained a Cuban passport in 2009 and returned to Cuba multiple times, thus voluntarily reavailed himself of Cuba's protection.

propositions.text: The Minister's cessation application is allowed and the respondent's refugee claim is deemed rejected under section 108(3) of the Act.

paragraphs.summary: The court allows the Minister's cessation application and deems the respondent's refugee claim rejected under section 108(3).

propositions.text: The hearing was set for February 1, 2018, but the respondent failed to appear.
The respondent's Notice to Appear was returned indicating he had moved.
The hearing proceeded in the respondent's absence based on several factors.

paragraphs.summary: The hearing was scheduled for February 1, 2018, but the respondent did not appear; the hearing proceeded in his absence.

propositions.text: The Minister sent the cessation application and documents to the respondent's last known address by regular mail on May 5, 2015.
On May 25, 2015, the RPD sent an acknowledgement and client contact form to the same address.
The respondent received the information and on June 16, 2015, requested a venue change, providing the same address.
The client contact form reminds respondents to notify parties of any address changes without delay.
The respondent's request for a venue change was granted.

paragraphs.summary: The Minister and RPD sent documents to the respondent's last known address, which he received and used to request a venue change, which was granted.

propositions.text: The respondent was aware of the cessation application and his duty to notify parties of contact information changes.
The respondent was not diligent in updating his contact information.
The RPD made documented efforts to locate the respondent after the Notice to Appear was returned undelivered.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the respondent knew of the cessation application and his duty to update contact info but was not diligent; RPD tried to locate him.

propositions.text: Rule 12 requires the protected person to notify the Division and Minister in writing of any contact information changes without delay.
The respondent knowingly failed to fulfill his duty under Rule 12.
Proceeding with the hearing in the respondent's absence does not breach procedural fairness.

paragraphs.summary: Rule 12 requires prompt notification of contact changes; the respondent failed this duty, so proceeding without him is fair.

propositions.text: Section 108(1)(a) states a claim is rejected if the person voluntarily reavailed themselves of their country's protection.

paragraphs.summary: Section 108(1)(a) provides refugee claims are rejected if the person voluntarily reavailed themselves of their country's protection.

propositions.text: The Minister argues the respondent obtained a Cuban passport after refugee status and returned to Cuba in 2011, 2013, and 2015.
The passport and travel stamps are in evidence.
In March 2015, the respondent confirmed these facts in a sworn statement to the Minister.

paragraphs.summary: The Minister argues the respondent obtained a Cuban passport and returned to Cuba multiple times, confirmed by evidence and the respondent's sworn statement.

propositions.text: The respondent states he returned to Cuba in 2011 due to his father's cancer and in 2013 for the funeral, providing supporting documents at the port of entry.
He returned in 2015 because his mother was hospitalized.
The Minister has not contradicted these explanations, which are accepted as credible.

paragraphs.summary: The respondent explains his returns to Cuba for family illness and funeral, supported by documents; the court accepts these as credible.

propositions.text: The UNHCR Handbook states cessation requires voluntariness, intention, and reavailment.
The respondent voluntarily obtained a passport and returned to Cuba without duress or coercion.
He was not forced or pressured to acquire a passport or return to Cuba.
He obtained the passport in 2009, before his father's illness, implying intention to be protected by Cuba.
No evidence explains his motivation for obtaining the passport.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the respondent voluntarily obtained a Cuban passport in 2009 before family illness, implying intention to be protected by Cuba.

propositions.text: The UNHCR Handbook presumes obtaining a national passport indicates intent to avail oneself of the country's protection, terminating refugee status absent proof otherwise.

paragraphs.summary: The UNHCR Handbook presumes obtaining a national passport indicates intent to avail oneself of that country's protection, ending refugee status.

propositions.text: Canadian jurisprudence presumes obtaining a passport from the country of nationality indicates reavailment of protection.
The respondent not only obtained a passport but returned to Cuba three times, reinforcing reavailment.
UNHCR Handbook states returning with a travel document from the refugee-granting country also indicates reavailment and loss of refugee status.

paragraphs.summary: Canadian law and UNHCR guidance presume obtaining a passport and returning to the country indicates reavailment and loss of refugee status.

propositions.text: The respondent's reasons for returning (family illness and funeral) are considered but do not rebut the presumption of reavailment.
UNHCR Handbook suggests visiting sick relatives may rebut reavailment presumption, unlike holidays or business trips.
No evidence shows the respondent sought permission or a Canadian travel document to travel to Cuba.
It is reasonable to expect a refugee to seek permission or discuss implications before returning to the country of persecution.
The respondent justified trips after returning rather than seeking permission beforehand.
Despite fear of Cuban authorities, the respondent reacquired a Cuban passport and traveled with it three times, creating multiple interactions with Cuban authorities.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the respondent's family reasons do not rebut reavailment; he did not seek Canadian permission and traveled with a Cuban passport multiple times.

propositions.text: The respondent's reasons do not overcome section 108(1)(a) given his early passport acquisition and travel without Canadian permission or travel document.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes the respondent's reasons do not overcome section 108(1)(a) due to early passport acquisition and travel without Canadian permission.

propositions.text: Section 108(1)(a) applies; the Minister's cessation application is allowed and the respondent's claim is rejected under section 108(3).

paragraphs.summary: The court applies section 108(1)(a), allows the Minister's cessation application, and rejects the respondent's claim under section 108(3).
